title: Reading First Clement

objectives.can: Read 1 Clement's periodic, rhetorical Greek and recognise Septuagint quotation within it.

explanation.summary: First Clement is a letter from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth, written about the end of the first century (the date is debated). Its Greek mixes two voices: long stretches of quotation from Scripture in the style of the Greek Old Testament, and Clement's own more rhetorical prose. Learning to hear the difference is the aim of this lesson.

sections.heading: Before you read: the text is analysed by machine
body: The analysis of First Clement in this library was made by a program and has not been checked by hand. Some words have no analysis, and some labels would be corrected by a Greek reader. The lesson therefore uses examples whose analysis is reliable and asks authored questions. When the program and the grammar disagree, trust the grammar.

sections.heading: Chapter 4: a quotation, then a comment
body: Chapter 4 begins with Γέγραπται γὰρ οὕτως, 'for it is written thus', and then retells the story of Cain and Abel. For about six sections Clement is giving the text of Genesis 4 as he knew it, in the Greek of the Septuagint. A Septuagint edition today may differ from his wording in places; ancient copies of the Greek Old Testament varied, and so did the way early Christian writers quoted.

At 4.7 Clement turns to his own voice: ὁρᾶτε, ἀδελφοί, 'see, brothers', and then a sentence with abstract nouns as its subject, ζῆλος καὶ φθόνος, 'jealousy and envy', as the cause of the first murder. The following sections line up more examples of ζῆλος, each beginning with ζῆλος or διὰ ζῆλος. This is rhetorical writing: the same word begins one sentence after another, and the examples are heaped up to make a case.

sections.heading: Marks of translation Greek
body: The quoted narrative is full of constructions that are common in the Greek Old Testament and in Luke and Acts, where they are often explained as imitating Hebrew narrative style. (This is the usual explanation; the details are discussed by scholars.)

First, καὶ ἐγένετο, 'and it came about', opens the story at 4.1 and again at 4.6. Second, ἐν τῷ with an infinitive and an accusative subject, as in ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτούς (4.6), 'while they were …', gives a time clause. Luke 5:12 has exactly Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτὸν. Third, sentences are linked by καί one after another (parataxis), where classical prose would use participles and subordinate clauses. Fourth, a pronoun is added where the article alone could have carried the sense: Ἄβελ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ (4.6), 'Abel his brother'. Greek of every period can add such a possessive, but it is especially frequent in translation Greek, and readers often point to Hebrew style as the reason. It is not an error.

sections.heading: Clement's own prose
body: In 4.10 Clement's own words surround a quotation: ζῆλος φυγεῖν ἠνάγκασεν Μωϋσῆν, 'jealousy compelled Moses to flee' (an accusative and infinitive after a verb of compelling), ἐν τῷ ἀκοῦσαι αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁμοφύλου, 'when he heard from his fellow countryman'. So ἐν τῷ + infinitive is not only in the quotation: Clement uses it himself. His habit of writing in biblical style is part of his voice.
Compare the long, balanced sentences of the classical world with this: Clement's chapters are built from repeated patterns, direct address (ἀδελφοί) and lists, which is what 'rhetorical' means here.

sections.heading: A tool for telling the voices apart
body: Look for the introduction (γέγραπται, εἶπεν), for narrative καὶ ἐγένετο, for a drift to direct speech without a verb of speaking, and for how often καί begins a sentence. Look then for the signs of the writer's own voice: vocatives like ἀδελφοί, abstract nouns as subjects, and sentences that comment instead of narrate.

misunderstandings: ἐν τῷ + infinitive does not mean 'in the' something. It is a set phrase for 'while' or 'when': the article makes the infinitive a noun, and ἐν gives it a time sense.
καὶ ἐγένετο does not mean that the clause is about 'becoming' in a philosophical sense. It is a narrative opener, 'and it happened'.
Not everything in a chapter of 1 Clement is a quotation. A quotation can be long, and Clement's comment can slip in without a break; the introductory word is your signal.
The program's analysis can be wrong. If a form looks odd, test it against the grammar.

deeper.heading: Which Septuagint?
body: The Septuagint was not one fixed book in the first century. Differences between Clement's quotations and printed Septuagint editions are therefore not automatically errors; they may reflect another manuscript tradition, a quotation from memory, or an adaptation. The Septuagint itself is not yet analysed in this library, so this lesson compares Clement only with his own prose and with the New Testament.

quoted.title: First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians
quoted.reference: Clement of Rome, First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians 4.1
quoted.english: For it is written thus:—And it came to pass after certain days that Cain offered to God a sacrifice of the fruits of the earth, and Abel himself also offered of the first-born of the sheep and of their fat.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: Γέγραπται is perfect passive, third person singular: 'it stands written'. It introduces the quotation. ἐγένετο, aorist (middle form), opens the narrative as καὶ ἐγένετο, 'and it happened'. ἤνεγκεν is aorist active of φέρω: 'he brought' an offering.

quoted.title: First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians
quoted.reference: Clement of Rome, First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians 4.6
quoted.english: And Cain said to Abel his brother, Let us go unto the plain. And it came to pass that, while they were in the plain, Cain rose up against Abel his brother and slew him.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: Διέλθωμεν is an aorist subjunctive, first person plural, used as an invitation: 'let us go over'. Then καὶ ἐγένετο again, with ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτούς, 'while they were': the infinitive εἶναι has its subject αὐτούς in the accusative. Luke 5:12 has the same phrase with a singular subject.

examples.analysis: Clement's own voice: the nominative φθόνος is half of a compound subject with ζῆλος, and κατειργάσατο is an aorist (middle form) of κατεργάζομαι, 'it brought about'. The abstract nouns are the grammatical subject, so the sentence reads like a general statement of cause. The noun ἀδελφοκτονίαν was not analysed by the program.

examples.analysis: The comment (ζῆλος φυγεῖν ἠνάγκασεν Μωϋσῆν) uses an infinitive, φυγεῖν, with Moses as its accusative subject. Then ἐν τῷ ἀκοῦσαι αὐτὸν, 'when he heard', with an aorist infinitive. The question quoted after it has the aorist κατέστησεν, 'set up', and the infinitive ἀνελεῖν, 'to kill'.
